title: A protein from a green alga lets scientists switch nerve cells on with a flash of light
body: On 5 October 2026 Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for optogenetics. It began with the alga *Chlamydomonas*, which swims towards light and reacts within half a millisecond. Hegemann guessed that a single protein both caught the light and opened a channel in the cell, and in frog eggs he and Nagel found it: **channelrhodopsin**, which opens when blue light hits it and lets positive ions rush in. A nerve signal starts with just such an inward rush, so when Deisseroth put the gene into rat nerve cells in 2005, flashes of blue light made them fire. Because the gene can be put into one chosen type of nerve cell, researchers can now switch particular circuits on in a living brain and see what they do, as the [Nobel Assembly’s background](https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2026/10/popular-medicineprize2026.pdf) explains.

slides.question: Light hits the eyespot of the alga Chlamydomonas. How many milliseconds until an electrical signal appears?
slides.explanation: Half a millisecond, as Peter Hegemann measured. In our eyes it takes at least 10 ms, because the signal passes through a chain of chemical steps first.

slides.alt: Animation on dark teal: a nerve cell lights up gold when a blue flash hits it. Green algae swim to light; a frog egg makes the algal protein; blue light opens a channel in a membrane and coral ions rush in. A trace shows one signal per flash, then none without the gene; a mouse, a brain, an eye.

slides.prompt: Tune the blue flashes so the nerve cell fires exactly once per flash, at 10 or more flashes a second.
slides.takeaway: Too short and the channel lets in too few ions; too long and the cell fires more than once. A few milliseconds is just right, and without the gene no flash does anything: the light works only through the algal channel.

slides.heading: From an alga to the brain

events.text: Blue light fires rat nerve cells

slides.question: Why did Hegemann suspect that a single protein in the alga did two jobs?
options: It reacted too fast for a chain
Its genes had not been found
slides.explanation: Light set off a signal in half a millisecond, over twenty times faster than in our eyes, where chemical steps come first. Something simpler had to catch the light and open the channel.
